griqualand-west-colony.t: The short-lived British Crown colony around the Kimberley diamond fields, the cradle of South Africa's mining industry.
griqualand-west-colony.o: After the 1871 Keate Award upheld Nicolaas Waterboer's claim to the diamond diggings of Griqualand West, Britain annexed the area. It was governed at first through the Cape and was proclaimed a separate Crown colony in 1873, with Richard Southey as lieutenant-governor and Kimberley, the town around the Big Hole, as its capital.
griqualand-west-colony.r: Tens of thousands of diggers and African migrant workers poured in. Claim holders were mostly white, and disputes over labour, permits and illicit diamond buying shaped politics. The Black Flag Rebellion of white diggers in 1875 forced Southey's recall. A Griqua and Tlhaping rising in 1878 was suppressed.
griqualand-west-colony.e: The colony was annexed to the Cape Colony in 1880. Its diamond fields became the base of Cecil Rhodes's De Beers company, and the methods used there, such as closed labour compounds, shaped South African mining.

grand-duchy-of-frankfurt.t: Napoleonic grand duchy centred on Frankfurt, created for Karl Theodor von Dalberg and destined for Napoleon's stepson.
grand-duchy-of-frankfurt.o: In 1810 Dalberg ceded Regensburg to Bavaria and in exchange received Hanau and Fulda. These were combined with Frankfurt, Aschaffenburg and Wetzlar to form the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt, with Napoleon's stepson Eugène de Beauharnais named as Dalberg's successor.
grand-duchy-of-frankfurt.r: The grand duchy was divided into four departments on the French model. A constitution of 1810 introduced the Napoleonic Code and equal rights, and the Jews of Frankfurt bought their civic equality in 1811. Frankfurt remained a major trading and banking centre, but the Continental System hurt trade and the state had to provide troops for Napoleon.
grand-duchy-of-frankfurt.e: After the battle of Leipzig Dalberg abdicated in October 1813, and Eugène never succeeded. The allies placed it under provisional administration; Frankfurt became a free city, while Hanau and Fulda went to the Electorate of Hesse and Aschaffenburg to Bavaria.

governorate-of-new-castile.t: The Spanish governorate granted to Francisco Pizarro, under which the conquest of the Inca Empire took place and Lima was founded.
governorate-of-new-castile.o: By the Capitulation of Toledo in 1529, Charles V named Francisco Pizarro governor and captain-general of New Castile, a strip extending 200 leagues south from the Santiago river in Ecuador. Pizarro sailed from Panama in 1530 and began the conquest of the Inca Empire, capturing Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532.
governorate-of-new-castile.r: New Castile was governed by Pizarro with his brothers Hernando, Gonzalo and Juan. He founded San Miguel de Piura in 1532 and the City of the Kings, Lima, in 1535. Lands and native people were divided into encomiendas among the conquerors. The boundary with Diego de Almagro's Governorate of New Toledo, especially the possession of Cusco, led to civil war, and Almagro was executed in 1538.
governorate-of-new-castile.e: Almagro's followers assassinated Pizarro in Lima in 1541. In 1542 the New Laws created the Viceroyalty of Peru, which absorbed New Castile and New Toledo under a viceroy. Lima remained the capital of Spanish South America for nearly three centuries.

gabali.t: Mountain people of the Lozère, clients of the Arverni, who gave their name to the Gévaudan.
gabali.o: The Gabali lived on the granite plateaus and valleys of the southern Massif Central, in the modern Lozère. Caesar names them as clients of the Arverni.
gabali.r: Pliny mentions their silver mines and their cheese, which was sold in Rome. No rulers or institutions are recorded.
gabali.e: They took part in the revolt of Vercingetorix in 52 BCE, attacking the Helvii on the border of the Province. Under Rome their chief town was Anderitum (Javols), and their name lived on in the medieval county and bishopric of Gévaudan.

geshur.t: Geshur, a small Aramaean kingdom on the north-east shore of the Sea of Galilee, tied by marriage to King David.
geshur.o: Geshur occupied the southern Golan and the north-eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee. It appears in the Hebrew Bible as an Aramaean kingdom of the 10th century BCE, and excavations at Bethsaida and Tel Hadar have revealed fortified towns of the period.
geshur.r: Bethsaida had a large city gate with a stele showing a bull-headed god. According to the Bible, King Talmai of Geshur gave his daughter Maacah in marriage to David of the United Kingdom of Israel; their son Absalom later took refuge in Geshur.
geshur.e: Geshur disappears from records in the 9th century BCE, probably absorbed by Aram-Damascus.

golden-horde.t: The Mongol khanate of the western steppe that ruled the Rus' principalities for over two centuries and grew rich on trade from Sarai.
golden-horde.o: Founded by Batu, son of Jochi, after the great western campaign of 1236 to 1242, the khanate took the steppe from the Danube to the Irtysh, with Sarai on the lower Volga as its capital. It ruled the conquered Rus' principalities through tribute and the grant of patents to princes.
golden-horde.r: Its khans ruled a largely Kipchak Turkic population, and Mongol rule merged into Turkic culture. Uzbek Khan made Islam the state religion in the early 14th century. Sarai became a large trading city on routes linking the Black Sea, Genoese Crimea, Central Asia and Egypt's Mamluks. The khans collected Rus' tribute through Muscovite grand princes.
golden-horde.e: From the 1360s civil war, the 'Great Troubles', and Timur's campaigns against Tokhtamysh in 1395 wrecked its economy. It broke into the Khanate of Kazan, the Crimean and Astrakhan Khanates and the Great Horde, and Moscow ended tribute after 1480.

grand-duchy-of-luxembourg.t: The world's only remaining grand duchy, created in 1815 and grown from a fortress state into a founding member of the European Union and a financial centre.
grand-duchy-of-luxembourg.o: The Congress of Vienna made the former Duchy of Luxembourg a grand duchy, held by William I of the Netherlands in personal union and a member of the German Confederation, with a Prussian garrison in its fortress. After the Belgian Revolution, the Treaty of London of 1839 gave its French-speaking western half to Belgium.
grand-duchy-of-luxembourg.r: The Treaty of London of 1867 made Luxembourg permanently neutral and its fortress was demolished. Personal union with the Netherlands ended in 1890, when Adolphe of Nassau-Weilburg became grand duke. Steel, based on local iron ore, made the country prosperous. Germany occupied it in both world wars, and Grand Duchess Charlotte led resistance from exile.
grand-duchy-of-luxembourg.e: After 1945 Luxembourg abandoned neutrality, co-founding Benelux, NATO and the European Communities and hosting European institutions. As steel declined it became a banking and investment centre. It remains a constitutional monarchy; Grand Duke Guillaume succeeded his father Henri in 2025.

genoese-pera.t: The Genoese colony of Galata across the Golden Horn from Constantinople, a merchant republic whose trade outstripped the Byzantine capital itself.
genoese-pera.o: The Treaty of Nymphaeum of 1261 rewarded Genoa for helping Michael VIII Palaiologos, and in 1267 the emperor granted the Genoese the suburb of Pera, or Galata, on the north side of the Golden Horn.
genoese-pera.r: Pera was governed by a podesta sent from Genoa, with its own councils and courts. It grew into the hub of Genoese trade with the Black Sea colonies such as Caffa, dealing in grain, slaves, alum and silk, and by the 14th century its customs revenues far exceeded those of Constantinople. The Genoese walled the town and in 1348 built the Tower of Christ, now the Galata Tower, and fought the Byzantines and Venetians for control of the straits.
genoese-pera.e: During the siege of 1453 Pera stayed officially neutral. After Constantinople fell it surrendered to Mehmed II, who guaranteed its residents' property and religion but dismantled its walls; Galata remained a centre of the European community.

gurgum.t: Gurgum, a Neo-Hittite kingdom centred on Maraş, whose kings left Luwian inscriptions and lion sculptures before Assyria annexed it.
gurgum.o: Gurgum arose after the Hittite collapse in the valley of the Aksu river around Marqas, modern Kahramanmaraş, in south-eastern Turkey. A local dynasty ruled it from the 10th century BCE or earlier.
gurgum.r: Its kings, several called Halparuntiya, left Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions on stelae and lion statues recording their family line and building works. Gurgum joined alliances with Sam'al and Arpad against the Assyrian Empire and paid tribute to it as circumstances required.
gurgum.e: King Tarhulara was murdered by his son Mutallu. In 711 BCE Sargon II of the Assyrian Empire deposed Mutallu and annexed Gurgum as the province of Marqasi.

grand-principality-of-transylvania.t: Habsburg crown land of Transylvania, where Hungarian, Saxon, Székely and Romanian communities contested rights until its union with Hungary in 1867.
grand-principality-of-transylvania.o: After the Peace of Szatmár in 1711 ended Francis II Rákóczi's revolt, Transylvania was governed directly by the Habsburgs as a separate land of the Hungarian Crown, under the Leopoldine Diploma of 1691. In 1765 Maria Theresa raised it to the rank of grand principality, and the Habsburg ruler took the title of grand prince.
grand-principality-of-transylvania.r: A gubernium answering to Vienna ran the land, sitting at Hermannstadt for much of the 18th century, with governors such as the Saxon Samuel von Brukenthal. The old system of three privileged nations persisted, leaving the Romanian majority without political rights, though the union of many Orthodox Romanians with Rome around 1700 opened schools at Blaj. Horea's peasant revolt of 1784 was bloodily suppressed.
grand-principality-of-transylvania.e: In 1848 Hungarian revolutionaries proclaimed union with Hungary while Romanians at Blaj demanded national rights, and civil war followed. After 1849 Transylvania was again a separate crown land, until the Compromise of 1867 merged it into the Kingdom of Hungary (1867-1918). It joined Romania in 1918.
grand-principality-of-transylvania.re: Orthodox, Greek Catholic, Catholic and Protestant Christianity

grand-duchy-of-moscow.t: Muscovy, the small appanage that gathered the Russian lands, threw off Tatar rule and became the core of the Russian state.
grand-duchy-of-moscow.o: Moscow, first mentioned in 1147, became the seat of its own prince around 1263, when Alexander Nevsky's youngest son Daniel received it. Daniel and his sons enlarged the territory, and in 1325 the head of the Russian church moved to Moscow. In 1331 Ivan I Kalita became the sole grand prince of Vladimir, collecting tribute for the Golden Horde.
grand-duchy-of-moscow.r: The grand princes built power by buying, conquering and inheriting neighbouring lands, aided by the church and loyal boyars. Dmitry Donskoy defeated the Tatars at Kulikovo in 1380. Ivan III annexed the Novgorod Republic and Tver, ended Horde overlordship at the Ugra river in 1480, rebuilt the Kremlin with Italian architects and issued a law code in 1497.
grand-duchy-of-moscow.e: Vasily III completed the absorption of Pskov and Ryazan. In 1547 his son Ivan IV was crowned tsar, and the grand duchy became the Tsardom of Russia, the direct ancestor of the Russian Empire.

grand-duchy-of-baden.t: South-western German grand duchy known for its liberal constitution, its revolutionaries of 1848-49 and its role as a model constitutional state.
grand-duchy-of-baden.o: Elector Charles Frederick of Baden joined the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806 and became grand duke, gaining Austrian Breisgau, mediatised lands and the Lake Constance region. His long, narrow state stretched from Mannheim to Constance along the Rhine.
grand-duchy-of-baden.r: The constitution of 1818 created one of the most liberal parliaments in Germany. The Baden revolutionaries of 1848, led by Friedrich Hecker and Gustav Struve, were defeated, and in 1849 the army mutinied and the grand duke fled until Prussian troops restored him. Under Frederick I, from 1856, Baden became a liberal model state. Universities at Heidelberg and Freiburg and industry at Mannheim and Karlsruhe flourished.
grand-duchy-of-baden.e: Baden sided with Austria in 1866 but joined the German Empire in 1871. Grand Duke Frederick II abdicated in November 1918, and the state became the Republic of Baden.

gela.t: Rhodian and Cretan colony on Sicily's south coast whose tyrants, Hippocrates and Gelon, built the first great Greek power on the island.
gela.o: Colonists from Lindos on Rhodes and from Crete, led by Antiphemus and Entimus, founded Gela around 689 BCE on a long ridge by the Gela river, inland of a sandy coast. The colony pushed into the Sicel interior and in 580 BCE founded Acragas to the west.
gela.r: Gela reached its peak under the tyrants Cleander and Hippocrates, who around 495 BCE dominated much of eastern Sicily, and under Gelon, who seized Syracuse in 485 BCE and moved half of Gela's people there. Its farmland produced grain and horses, and its terracotta workshops and coins with a man-headed bull were renowned. The playwright Aeschylus died there in 456 BCE.
gela.e: Carthage sacked Gela in 405 BCE. Timoleon resettled it in the 330s BCE, but in 282 BCE Phintias, tyrant of Acragas, destroyed it and moved its people to his new city at Licata. The site was refounded by Frederick II in 1233 as Terranova, renamed Gela in 1927.

gaetuli.t: Berber pastoral peoples of the Saharan fringe south of Numidia and Mauretania, feared by Rome as raiders and prized as cavalry.
gaetuli.o: The Gaetuli are known from Roman writers such as Sallust and Strabo, who used the name for the nomadic and semi-nomadic Berber peoples living along the Saharan Atlas, from southern Morocco to southern Tunisia. They appear in the record from the 2nd century BCE.
gaetuli.r: They had no single government but lived in tribes under chiefs, herding horses, sheep and goats and moving with the seasons. They served as cavalry for Jugurtha and for Julius Caesar, and some received Roman citizenship. Gaetulian purple dye from the Atlantic coast was prized in Rome. They paid tribute to the Kingdom of Mauretania.
gaetuli.e: Around 6 CE they rebelled against Juba II and were defeated by Cossus Cornelius Lentulus, who took the title Gaetulicus. In later centuries the name faded, and the peoples it described merged with other Berber groups of the desert edge.

goshen.t: A tiny Boer freebooter republic on the Tswana border, whose land grab provoked Britain to take over southern Bechuanaland.
goshen.o: In 1882 white volunteers who had fought for the Barolong chief Moshette against Montshiwa were rewarded with farms, and they proclaimed the Land Goshen with its headquarters at Rooigrond, near Mafikeng. Its administrator was Gey van Pittius.
goshen.r: Goshen had little more than a few hundred settlers, raiding Montshiwa's cattle and land. It sought union with the South African Republic, which proclaimed a protectorate in 1884; Britain objected because the territory lay on the 'missionaries' road' to the interior.
goshen.e: The Warren Expedition of 1884-1885 dispersed the freebooters without a fight, and the land was incorporated into British Bechuanaland in 1885.

greco-bactrian-kingdom.t: The easternmost Hellenistic kingdom, where Greek kings ruled Bactria's 'thousand cities' and struck some of the finest coins of the ancient world.
greco-bactrian-kingdom.o: Bactria was a satrapy of the Seleucid Empire after Alexander the Great's conquest. Around 256 BCE its governor Diodotus I broke away, and his son Diodotus II ruled as an independent king. Euthydemus I then seized the throne and withstood a two-year siege of Bactra by Antiochus III, who recognised him as king around 206 BCE.
greco-bactrian-kingdom.r: Greek and Macedonian settlers formed the ruling class over a largely Iranian population, with cities such as Ai-Khanoum on the Amu Darya featuring a theatre, gymnasium and palace in Greek style. Irrigated farming and trade supported the state. Under Demetrius I the kings crossed the Hindu Kush into India, founding the Indo-Greek kingdoms, while Eucratides I ruled a vast territory in the 2nd century BCE.
greco-bactrian-kingdom.e: After Eucratides was murdered around 145 BCE, nomad invasions by the Saka and the Yuezhi overran Bactria, and Ai-Khanoum was abandoned. Greek rule continued south of the Hindu Kush in the Indo-Greek kingdoms until about 10 CE, and Greek script lived on in Kushan coinage.

governorate-of-livonia.t: Russian imperial province covering northern Latvia and southern Estonia, home to Riga and the University of Dorpat, where both Latvian and Estonian nationalism took shape.
governorate-of-livonia.o: Russia took Swedish Livonia in the Great Northern War; Riga fell in 1710, and the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 confirmed the conquest. The new province, at first called the Riga Governorate, covered Latvian Vidzeme, southern Estonia and, later, the island of Ösel.
governorate-of-livonia.r: The Livonian knighthood kept control of local government and the Lutheran church under the Baltic special order. Serfdom was abolished in 1819. The University of Dorpat, reopened in 1802, became a centre of Baltic German and later Estonian learning, and Riga grew into one of the empire's main industrial cities and ports. Latvian and Estonian national movements flourished, and Russification in the 1880s challenged German dominance.
governorate-of-livonia.e: In 1917 its northern part joined the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia. German forces occupied the rest in 1917-1918, and the Baltic Germans planned the United Baltic Duchy. After the war the territory was divided between the Republic of Latvia and the Republic of Estonia.

grey-league.t: The largest of the Three Leagues of the Grisons, a federation of upper Rhine valley communes sworn under a maple tree at Truns in 1424.
grey-league.o: In 1395 the abbot of Disentis and local lords of the upper Rhine valley made an alliance for peace and mutual protection, and in 1424 it was renewed at Truns, under a maple tree, as a league that included the communes themselves. The name Grey League is traditionally explained by the grey homespun cloth worn by its people.
grey-league.r: The league joined communes of the Surselva, Hinterrhein and Mesolcina valleys, each with its own courts and assembly, meeting at Ilanz. It allied with the League of God's House in 1406 and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions in 1471, forming the Three Leagues, and in 1497 became an associate of the Swiss. Its communes divided between Catholic and Reformed.
grey-league.e: The Grisons became part of the Helvetic Republic in 1799 and a Swiss canton in 1803. The league's name survives in Graubünden, the canton's German name.

gangani-britain.t: People of the Llŷn peninsula in north-west Wales, known from a headland Ptolemy named after them, with namesakes in western Ireland.
gangani-britain.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 names a Ganganorum Promontorium, the headland of the Gangani, on the coast of north-west Wales, generally identified with the tip of the Llŷn peninsula. Ptolemy does not list the Gangani among the inland peoples, so they may have been a small coastal group or a subdivision of the Ordovices.
gangani-britain.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Llŷn was a land of hillforts such as Tre'r Ceiri, a stone-walled settlement occupied into the Roman period, and of farming and fishing communities. The identical name in Ireland, borne by the Gangani (Ireland) on the Shannon, has prompted theories of migration across the Irish Sea in either direction.
gangani-britain.e: The Gangani are not mentioned again. Llŷn later saw Irish settlement in the post-Roman period and became part of the Kingdom of Gwynedd.

governorate-of-estonia.t: Russian imperial province of northern Estonia, governed for nearly two centuries by Baltic German nobles and the setting of the Estonian national awakening.
governorate-of-estonia.o: After Peter the Great conquered the Swedish Duchy of Estonia (1561-1721) in the Great Northern War, the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 made it a province of the Russian Empire, with Reval as its capital. Peter confirmed the privileges of the Baltic German nobility, their Lutheran church and German as the language of administration.
governorate-of-estonia.r: Under this Baltic special order, the Estonian knighthood ran local government, courts and the land, while Estonian peasants were serfs. Serfdom was abolished in 1816, though land remained with the nobles. In the late 19th century an Estonian national movement grew, and the Russification policies of the 1880s replaced German with Russian in schools and courts. Reval became an industrial port and naval base.
governorate-of-estonia.e: After the February Revolution of 1917 the Russian Provisional Government merged the governorate with the Estonian-speaking north of the Governorate of Livonia to form the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia, the forerunner of the Republic of Estonia.

great-horde.t: The last remnant of the Golden Horde on the lower Volga, whose khan Ahmad's retreat from the Ugra River in 1480 ended Mongol overlordship of Russia.
great-horde.o: By the mid-15th century the Golden Horde had shed the Khanate of Kazan, the Crimean Khanate and other states. The rump around Sarai, ruled by Küchük Muhammad and his sons, became known as the Great Horde, claiming to be the senior Jochid state.
great-horde.r: Its khans still demanded tribute from Moscow and fought the Crimean Khanate for the Golden Horde's heritage, allying with Poland-Lithuania. Akhmed Khan, or Ahmad, was its strongest ruler. Its nomadic economy suffered as trade shifted and the Volga cities declined.
great-horde.e: In 1480 Ahmad faced Ivan III's army on the Ugra River and withdrew without battle, ending Muscovy's tribute. He was killed in 1481 by Ibak Khan of the Tyumen Khanate. In 1502 the Crimean khan Meñli I Giray sacked Sarai and destroyed the horde.

government-of-national-salvation.t: Collaborationist Serbian government of General Milan Nedić, which administered German-occupied Serbia during the Second World War.
government-of-national-salvation.o: After the Axis conquest of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in April 1941, a reduced Serbia was placed under a German military commander. A commissioner government led by Milan Aćimović proved unable to cope with the uprising of summer 1941, and on 29 August 1941 the Germans installed the former war minister General Milan Nedić at the head of a Government of National Salvation.
government-of-national-salvation.r: The government ran the civil administration, police and a Serbian State Guard, but the German occupiers held real power and carried out mass reprisals, such as the Kragujevac massacre of October 1941. Jews of Serbia were murdered in 1941 and 1942, with the help of local police. Nedić promoted a conservative peasant ideology and sheltered refugees from the Independent State of Croatia.
government-of-national-salvation.e: As Partisans and the Soviet Red Army advanced, Nedić fled in October 1944 and Belgrade was liberated. He died in Yugoslav custody in 1946. The regime's record of collaboration remains debated in Serbia.

german-south-west-africa.t: Germany's colony in Namibia, a settler territory where the colonial army committed genocide against the Herero and Nama.
german-south-west-africa.o: In 1883 the Bremen merchant Adolf Lüderitz bought land at Angra Pequena, and on 24 April 1884 Germany declared a protectorate. Protection treaties with the Herero Paramountcy and the Rehoboth Basters followed, and Curt von François founded Windhoek as the capital in 1890.
german-south-west-africa.r: Governor Theodor Leutwein ruled through treaties with chiefs while settlers took land and cattle. The Herero rising of 1904 and the Nama war under Hendrik Witbooi were crushed by General Lothar von Trotha; tens of thousands died in the desert and in concentration camps such as Shark Island. Diamonds found near Lüderitz in 1908 made the colony profitable.
german-south-west-africa.e: South African forces invaded during the First World War, and the German garrison surrendered at Khorab in July 1915. The territory became South West Africa. Germany formally acknowledged the genocide in 2021.

governorate-of-courland.t: Russian imperial province formed from the Duchy of Courland in 1795, ruled by its Baltic German knighthood until the First World War.
governorate-of-courland.o: After the Third Partition of Poland in 1795, the nobility of the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia submitted to Catherine the Great, and the duchy, with the District of Pilten, became the Governorate of Courland, with its capital at Mitau (Jelgava).
governorate-of-courland.r: The Courland knighthood kept control of local government, courts and the Lutheran church under the Baltic special order, and German remained the language of administration until the Russification of the 1880s. Serfdom was abolished in 1817, but the land stayed largely with the nobles. Latvian peasants increasingly bought farms, and Libau (Liepāja) and Windau grew as ports. The 1905 revolution saw many manor houses burned.
governorate-of-courland.e: German armies occupied Courland in 1915, and it was administered by Ober Ost. In 1918 the Baltic Germans proclaimed the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia (1918), but after Germany's defeat the territory became part of the Republic of Latvia, with a small southern strip going to Lithuania.

governorate-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.t: The first Spanish governorate of the River Plate basin, which founded Buenos Aires and Asunción and opened the interior of southern South America.
governorate-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.o: In 1534 Charles V granted Pedro de Mendoza a governorate south of Pizarro's lands. Mendoza founded Buenos Aires in 1536, but hunger and attacks forced its abandonment in 1541. Juan de Salazar founded Asunción in 1537, upriver on the Paraguay river, and it became the capital of the governorate.
governorate-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.r: From Asunción, governors such as Domingo Martínez de Irala and Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca ruled a frontier colony built on alliances with the Guaraní, many of whom were bound in encomiendas, and on mixed marriages that produced a large mestizo population. Expeditions sought a route to the silver of Peru. Juan de Garay founded Santa Fe in 1573 and refounded Buenos Aires in 1580. Hernandarias, the first Creole governor, promoted Jesuit missions.
governorate-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.e: In 1617 the crown split the vast governorate into the Governorate of Paraguay, based at Asunción, and the Governorate of Buenos Aires. Both later joined the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata created in 1776, and Asunción is remembered as the 'mother of cities' for the towns founded from it.

gaza.t: Gaza, the southernmost Philistine city and the gateway between Egypt and Asia, a hub of the incense trade that resisted Alexander.
gaza.o: Gaza was the main Egyptian administrative base in Canaan during the Late Bronze Age. In the 12th century BCE Philistines settled there, and it became one of the cities of the Philistine Pentapolis, controlling the coastal road to Egypt.
gaza.r: Its kings grew rich as the terminus of caravan routes from Arabia carrying frankincense and myrrh. The Bible sets the death of Samson in its temple of Dagon. In 734 BCE King Hanunu fled to Egypt before Tiglath-Pileser III of the Assyrian Empire, who made Gaza a trading post.
gaza.e: Under the Achaemenid Empire Gaza was a flourishing frontier city. In 332 BCE its commander Batis held out against Alexander of the Macedonian Empire for two months; the city was stormed and its people killed or enslaved.

grenland.t: Petty kingdom at the mouth of the Skien river in southern Norway, one of the coastal realms brought under Harald Fairhair.
grenland.o: Grenland, around the lower Skienselva and the coast of modern Telemark, appears in the sagas as one of the small kingdoms of south-eastern Norway. Its early history is obscure and known only from scattered references in later Icelandic writings.
grenland.r: The district looked to the sea and the Skagerrak, and its people farmed, fished and traded. Inland Telemark supplied iron and whetstones that were exported widely in the Viking Age. No reliable record of its kings or institutions survives.
grenland.e: Grenland passed into the realm of the Vestfold kings and of Harald Fairhair in the late 9th century and became part of the Kingdom of Norway. The town of Skien grew there in the Middle Ages.

griqualand-east.t: The territory where Adam Kok III's Griqua resettled after their trek over the Drakensberg, with its capital at Kokstad.
griqualand-east.o: After selling their land at Philippolis to the Orange Free State in 1861, Adam Kok III and some 2,000 Griqua trekked across the Drakensberg with wagons and cattle, arriving in 1863 in Nomansland, a thinly settled area between the Mpondo Kingdom and Natal that the Cape government had offered them.
griqualand-east.r: The Griqua set up a Volksraad under Kok, issued land titles and coined their own small currency. They founded Kokstad in 1869 below Mount Currie. Many settlers, however, sold their farms to whites, and debt and land loss weakened the community.
griqualand-east.e: The Cape Colony took over administration in 1874 and annexed the territory formally in 1879, after Kok's death in 1875 and a short Griqua rising in 1878. Kokstad remains a centre of Griqua identity.

grand-duchy-of-lithuania.t: Once the largest state in Europe, a pagan Baltic power that grew to rule most of Belarus and Ukraine and joined Poland in the Commonwealth.
grand-duchy-of-lithuania.o: In the early 13th century Lithuanian chiefs united against attacks by German crusaders and their neighbours, and in 1236 a Lithuanian army destroyed the Livonian Brothers of the Sword at Saule. Mindaugas unified the tribes and was crowned king in 1253, briefly creating the Kingdom of Lithuania, before the grand ducal state took its lasting form.
grand-duchy-of-lithuania.r: Gediminas, who ruled from about 1316 to 1341, made Vilnius his capital and expanded into Rus', and his sons Algirdas and Kestutis took Kiev and much of the Dnieper basin. Lithuania stayed pagan until Jogaila's baptism in 1387. Ruthenian was the chancery language, the Lithuanian Statutes codified law, and Orthodox, Catholics, Jews and Tatars lived side by side.
grand-duchy-of-lithuania.e: Vytautas helped defeat the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410. Long tied to Poland by personal unions, the grand duchy joined it in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth by the Union of Lublin in 1569, keeping its own army, treasury and law. The Third Partition of 1795 gave its lands to the Russian Empire.
grand-duchy-of-lithuania.re: Baltic paganism, later Catholic and Orthodox Christianity

gabon-french-colony.t: French rule over the Gabon estuary and its hinterland, from coastal treaty posts in the 1840s to an autonomous republic in 1958.
gabon-french-colony.o: French naval officers signed treaties with Mpongwe rulers of the Gabon estuary, including King Denis Rapontchombo in 1839 and King Louis in 1842, and built a fort in 1843 to support anti-slave-trade patrols. Libreville was founded in 1849 by Africans freed from a captured slave ship. Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza's expeditions from the 1870s pushed claims inland.
gabon-french-colony.r: Gabon was long administered with the French Congo and from 1910 as part of French Equatorial Africa. Concession companies, timber cutting, especially of okoumé, and forced labour shaped the economy, while Catholic and Protestant missions spread schooling. Albert Schweitzer ran his hospital at Lambaréné from 1913.
gabon-french-colony.e: In 1958 Gabon became an autonomous republic within the French Community and gained full independence on 17 August 1960 under Léon M'ba.

gcaleka-xhosa-kingdom.t: The senior Xhosa kingdom east of the Kei, whose rulers Hintsa and Sarhili faced British expansion and the catastrophe of the cattle-killing.
gcaleka-xhosa-kingdom.o: When the united Xhosa Kingdom divided around 1775, the Great House under Gcaleka kept the senior paramountcy and the lands east of the Kei river, while the Rharhabe Xhosa Kingdom held the west. Gcaleka's successors continued to be recognised as paramount over all Xhosa.
gcaleka-xhosa-kingdom.r: The paramount ruled his own chiefdom directly and held ritual seniority over others, governing with councillors. Hintsa was drawn into the Sixth Frontier War and was shot while held by British forces in 1835. Under Sarhili, the Gcaleka followed the prophecies of Nongqawuse in 1856–57, killing their cattle in hope of deliverance, which led to mass famine.
gcaleka-xhosa-kingdom.e: After the Ninth Frontier War of 1877–78, Sarhili was driven out and Gcalekaland came under Cape control, being formally annexed by 1885. The Xhosa royal house continues, and the cattle-killing remains a defining memory in South African history.

grand-duchy-of-berg.t: Napoleonic model state on the lower Rhine, ruled first by Joachim Murat and used to spread French law in Germany.
grand-duchy-of-berg.o: The Duchy of Berg on the right bank of the Rhine belonged to Bavaria, which ceded it to Napoleon in 1806. He combined it with Cleves and other lands and gave it to his brother-in-law Joachim Murat as the Grand Duchy of Berg, with Düsseldorf as capital.
grand-duchy-of-berg.r: When Murat became King of Naples in 1808, Napoleon ruled Berg himself on behalf of his young nephew Napoleon Louis. The grand duchy was organised in French-style departments, abolished serfdom and introduced the Napoleonic Code. The industrial region of Elberfeld and Barmen, with textile and metal trades, suffered from the Continental System, which cut it off from British markets, and conscription led to riots in 1813.
grand-duchy-of-berg.e: After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig, allied troops took Berg in late 1813. It was placed under provisional administration, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave it to Prussia as part of the Rhine Province.

germiyanids.t: A powerful beylik of western Anatolia centred on Kutahya, important patrons of early Anatolian Turkish literature.
germiyanids.o: The Germiyan were a tribal group settled by the Seljuks near Malatya and moved to the Kutahya region in the later 13th century to guard the frontier. As Seljuk authority waned around 1300, their leaders ruled Kutahya as an independent beylik, for a time the strongest in western Anatolia.
germiyanids.r: Yakub I received tribute from several neighbours, including Byzantine Philadelphia, and absorbed the Inancid and Sahib Ataid lands. Suleyman Shah married his daughter to the future Bayezid I, giving Kutahya as part of her dowry around 1381. The court sponsored poets writing in Turkish, among them Ahmedi and Sheykhoglu Mustafa, and the alum and other mines of the region brought wealth.
germiyanids.e: Bayezid I took the rest of the beylik in 1390, but Timur restored Yakub II in 1402. Yakub II bequeathed his lands to Murad II, and they passed to the Ottomans on his death in 1429.

galatia.t: Galatia, the land of three Celtic tribes who crossed into Anatolia in 278 BCE and kept their own language and laws for centuries.
galatia.o: In 278 BCE Nicomedes I of the Kingdom of Bithynia invited bands of Celtic warriors across the Bosporus as mercenaries. After years of raiding western Anatolia, they were defeated by Antiochus I and Attalus I of the Kingdom of Pergamon and settled on the central plateau around Ancyra.
galatia.r: Three tribes, the Tolistobogii, Tectosages and Trocmi, each split into four parts under tetrarchs, met in a council of 300 at a sacred grove called Drynemeton. Galatians served as mercenaries across the Hellenistic world. The statues of the Dying Gaul commemorate Pergamon's victories over them.
galatia.e: In the 1st century BCE Deiotarus, Rome's ally, made himself king of all Galatia. After the death of the last king, Amyntas, in 25 BCE, Augustus made Galatia a Roman province; Paul later wrote to its Christian communities.

gaza-empire.t: The Nguni conquest state of southern Mozambique founded by Soshangane, the last great African power to resist Portugal in the region.
gaza-empire.o: Soshangane, a commander of Zwide's Ndwandwe Kingdom, fled north after the Ndwandwe defeat by the Zulu and by about 1824 had settled in southern Mozambique. He conquered Tsonga and Chopi communities and defeated Portuguese posts at Delagoa Bay and Inhambane, building a kingdom that reached the Zambezi and the eastern Zimbabwe highlands.
gaza-empire.r: The Nguni elite ruled through age regiments on the Zulu model, taking tribute in cattle and young men from conquered peoples, who became known as Shangaan. A long succession war after Soshangane's death in 1858 brought his son Mzila to power. Later rulers profited from sending men to work on the Kimberley and Witwatersrand mines.
gaza-empire.e: Ngungunhane moved the capital to Mandlakazi in 1889 and tried to play Britain against Portugal. Portuguese forces defeated his army at Coolela in 1895 and captured him at Chaimite; he died in exile in the Azores, and the land became part of Portuguese Mozambique.

governorate-of-buenos-aires.t: The Spanish governorate around the River Plate estuary whose port, long restricted by Spain, thrived on smuggling and grew into a viceregal capital.
governorate-of-buenos-aires.o: In 1617 the Governorate of the Río de la Plata was divided, and the southern part became the Governorate of Buenos Aires, with its capital at Buenos Aires, refounded by Juan de Garay in 1580. It included the towns of Santa Fe, Corrientes and later Montevideo.
governorate-of-buenos-aires.r: Spain restricted trade through Buenos Aires to protect the official route through Lima and Panama, but the port flourished on smuggling of silver from Potosí in exchange for European goods and enslaved Africans. Cattle hides were the main export. Rivalry with Portugal over Colonia del Sacramento dominated its politics, and Governor Bruno Mauricio de Zabala founded Montevideo in 1724 to block Portuguese expansion.
governorate-of-buenos-aires.e: In 1776 Charles III made Buenos Aires the capital of the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, which absorbed the governorate. The port's growing importance laid the foundations for Argentina's later dominance in the region.

greater-lebanon.t: The French-created state that enlarged Mount Lebanon with Beirut, the coast and the Beqaa, giving Lebanon its modern borders.
greater-lebanon.o: On 1 September 1920 General Henri Gouraud proclaimed the State of Greater Lebanon in Beirut. Responding to the wishes of the Maronite Patriarch Elias Hoayek and others, France added Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon, Tyre and the Beqaa Valley to the former Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate.
greater-lebanon.r: The state was administered by French governors under the high commissioner, with an elected representative council from 1922 organised on confessional lines. The enlargement made it economically viable but brought in large Sunni and Shia populations, many of whom wanted union with Syria. Beirut became the seat of the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon.
greater-lebanon.e: In May 1926 a constitution was adopted that turned the state into the Lebanese Republic, with Charles Debbas as its first president.
greater-lebanon.re: Maronite Christianity, Sunni and Shia Islam, Druze

ganzhou-uyghur-kingdom.t: A Uyghur khaganate in the Hexi Corridor, founded by refugees from the fallen steppe empire, that controlled a key stretch of the Silk Road for over a century.
ganzhou-uyghur-kingdom.o: When the Uyghur Khaganate in Mongolia was destroyed by the Kyrgyz in 840, Uyghur groups fled south and west. One group settled among the oases of the Hexi Corridor and by the 890s had made Ganzhou (modern Zhangye) the seat of its own khagan.
ganzhou-uyghur-kingdom.r: The khagans ruled Uyghur herders alongside Chinese, Tibetan and other townspeople, profiting from the horse and jade trade between Central Asia and China. They sent tribute missions to the Five Dynasties courts and the Song Dynasty, intermarried with the Cao rulers of the Guiyi Circuit at Dunhuang and sometimes fought them. Buddhism largely replaced the Manichaeism of the old khaganate.
ganzhou-uyghur-kingdom.e: Rising Tangut power closed in, and in 1028 Li Yuanhao, later founder of Western Xia, captured Ganzhou. Uyghur remnants survived in the region; the Yugur (Yellow Uyghur) people of Gansu are commonly regarded as their descendants.

governorate-of-tucuman.t: The Spanish governorate of northwestern Argentina, a chain of towns linking the River Plate to the silver mines of Upper Peru.
governorate-of-tucuman.o: Spanish settlers from Peru and Chile founded Santiago del Estero in 1553, the oldest surviving city in Argentina. In 1563 Philip II created the Governorate of Tucumán, Juríes and Diaguitas, separating it from Chile and placing it under the Audiencia of Charcas, with Santiago del Estero as capital.
governorate-of-tucuman.r: Governors founded a series of towns, including San Miguel de Tucumán in 1565, Córdoba in 1573, Salta in 1582 and San Salvador de Jujuy in 1593. The economy supplied mules, cattle, textiles and foodstuffs to Potosí. The Diaguita and Calchaquí peoples resisted in the Calchaquí Wars until the 1660s. The Jesuits founded the University of Córdoba in 1613, the oldest in Argentina, and ran estancias in the region.
governorate-of-tucuman.e: Tucumán became part of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776. In 1782 the intendancy reform divided it into the intendancies of Salta del Tucumán and Córdoba del Tucumán, which later became the provinces of northwestern Argentina.

governorate-of-new-toledo.t: The Spanish governorate granted to Diego de Almagro south of Pizarro's lands, whose disputed border over Cusco sparked the civil wars of the conquerors.
governorate-of-new-toledo.o: In 1534 Charles V granted Diego de Almagro, Francisco Pizarro's partner in the conquest of Peru, a governorate of 200 leagues south of the Governorate of New Castile. In 1535 Almagro led a large expedition south into Chile, crossing the Andes with Spanish soldiers and thousands of indigenous auxiliaries, but found no rich lands.
governorate-of-new-toledo.r: New Toledo was more a claim than an administered territory. Its northern boundary was vague, and Almagro insisted that Cusco lay within it. Returning from Chile in 1537, he seized Cusco from Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro during the rebellion of Manco Inca. War between the two factions followed.
governorate-of-new-toledo.e: Almagro was defeated at the Battle of Las Salinas in 1538 and executed. His son, Diego de Almagro the Younger, had Pizarro murdered in 1541 but was defeated at Chupas in 1542 and executed. That year the New Laws merged both governorates into the Viceroyalty of Peru.

grand-principality-of-serbia.t: Medieval Serbian state of Raška, where Stefan Nemanja united the Serbian lands and founded the dynasty that ruled Serbia for two centuries.
grand-principality-of-serbia.o: As Duklja declined in the late 11th century, Raška in the inland highlands gained independence under Grand Župan Vukan, who from about 1091 raided Byzantine territory. His successors of the Vukanović line ruled from Ras, often as Byzantine or Hungarian clients.
grand-principality-of-serbia.r: The grand župan ruled with regional lords (župans) and an assembly of nobles. Stefan Nemanja (1166–1196) defeated his brothers, annexed Duklja, Travunia and Zachlumia around 1186, and founded Studenica monastery. His youngest son, Rastko, became the monk Sava and helped establish Serbian Orthodox monasticism at Hilandar on Mount Athos. Byzantine and Hungarian pressure shaped its politics.
grand-principality-of-serbia.e: Nemanja abdicated in 1196 in favour of his son Stefan, who received a royal crown from Pope Honorius III in 1217. The state became the Kingdom of Serbia (medieval), ruled by the Nemanjić dynasty.

grand-principality-of-tver.t: Moscow's great rival for leadership of north-eastern Russia, whose princes held the throne of Vladimir before Moscow annexed Tver in 1485.
grand-principality-of-tver.o: Tver, on the upper Volga, received its first prince around 1247, when Yaroslav Yaroslavich, a younger brother of Alexander Nevsky, made it his seat. Yaroslav became grand prince of Vladimir in 1264, and Tver quickly grew into one of the strongest towns of the Vladimir-Suzdal lands.
grand-principality-of-tver.r: Tver controlled Volga trade and built early stone churches and fortifications. Mikhail Yaroslavich became grand prince of Vladimir in 1305 but was executed at the Golden Horde in 1318 after a struggle with Moscow. In 1327 a revolt in Tver killed the Mongol envoy Cholkhan, and Ivan Kalita of Moscow joined the Tatars in crushing it. The merchant Afanasy Nikitin set out from Tver for India in the 1460s.
grand-principality-of-tver.e: Under Boris Alexandrovich Tver revived in the 15th century, but it was surrounded by Moscow's territory. When its last prince, Mikhail Borisovich, sought Lithuanian help, Ivan III besieged the city and annexed it to the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1485.

generalitat-of-catalonia-1931-1939.t: Catalonia's autonomous government under the Second Republic, restored after two centuries and abolished after Franco's victory.
generalitat-of-catalonia-1931-1939.o: On 14 April 1931 Francesc Macià of the Republican Left of Catalonia proclaimed a Catalan Republic in Barcelona. After negotiations with Madrid it became an autonomous government that took the medieval name of the Generalitat, and the Statute of Autonomy was approved in 1932.
generalitat-of-catalonia-1931-1939.r: The Generalitat had its own parliament and powers over education, culture, public order and civil law, and promoted the Catalan language. Lluís Companys succeeded Macià in 1933. In October 1934 Companys proclaimed a Catalan State within a federal republic, leading to his arrest and the statute's suspension until 1936. During the civil war it ran much of the Republican war effort in Catalonia.
generalitat-of-catalonia-1931-1939.e: Nationalist forces took Barcelona in January 1939, and Franco abolished the autonomy. Companys was handed over by the Gestapo and executed in 1940. The Generalitat survived in exile and was restored in 1977.

genoese-gazaria.t: Genoa's string of trading colonies on the Crimean coast, centred on Caffa, a hub of the Black Sea slave, grain and silk trades.
genoese-gazaria.o: After the restoration of the Byzantine Empire in 1261 gave Genoa access to the Black Sea, Genoese merchants obtained the right to settle at Caffa, modern Feodosia, from the khan of the Golden Horde around 1266. Over the next century they added Soldaia, now Sudak, in 1365 and Cembalo, now Balaklava.
genoese-gazaria.r: Caffa was governed by a consul sent from Genoa and supervised by the Office of Gazaria there. Its merchants traded grain, fish, furs and especially slaves, many sold to Mamluk Egypt, as well as silk and spices from the Silk Road. Relations with the Golden Horde were tense: during a siege by Jani Beg in 1346 plague broke out, and ships from Caffa may have helped carry it to Europe.
genoese-gazaria.e: After 1453 Genoa handed the colonies to the Bank of San Giorgio, as the Ottoman Empire controlled the straits. In 1475 an Ottoman fleet under Gedik Ahmed Pasha took Caffa and the other colonies, ending Italian rule in the Crimea.

guiyi-circuit.t: The self-governing Chinese regime at Dunhuang that threw off Tibetan rule in 848 and whose rulers sponsored many of the Mogao caves and their famous manuscripts.
guiyi-circuit.o: In 848, as the Tibetan Empire disintegrated, the local leader Zhang Yichao drove the Tibetan garrison out of Dunhuang (Shazhou) and soon of other Hexi Corridor towns. He sent envoys to the Tang court, which in 851 recognised him as military governor of the Guiyi ('Return to Allegiance') Army.
guiyi-circuit.r: Though nominally a Tang and later Five Dynasties province, it was a hereditary oasis state, first under the Zhang family and from 914 under the Cao family, who married into the Khotanese and Uyghur royal houses. Its rulers financed cave temples at Mogao, and its monasteries produced the Dunhuang manuscripts in Chinese, Tibetan, Khotanese, Sogdian and Uyghur. Neighbours such as the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom often threatened it.
guiyi-circuit.e: Cao rule weakened in the early 11th century, and around 1036 the Western Xia took Dunhuang; the details of the final years are debated. The cave library, sealed around this time, was rediscovered in 1900.

government-of-the-grand-national-assembl.t: The Ankara government of Mustafa Kemal, which won the Turkish War of Independence and replaced the Ottoman Empire with the Turkish Republic.
government-of-the-grand-national-assembl.o: After the Allies formally occupied Constantinople in March 1920, nationalist deputies and delegates met in Ankara and on 23 April 1920 opened the Grand National Assembly, which claimed sovereignty in the name of the nation. Mustafa Kemal was elected its president.
government-of-the-grand-national-assembl.r: The assembly governed directly through ministers it elected and adopted a constitution in 1921 vesting sovereignty in the nation. It rejected the Treaty of Sevres, signed treaties with Soviet Russia at Moscow and Kars, and secured French withdrawal by the Treaty of Ankara. Its army stopped the Greeks at Sakarya in 1921 and drove them out in 1922 under Mustafa Kemal and Ismet.
government-of-the-grand-national-assembl.e: The assembly abolished the Ottoman sultanate in November 1922, won recognition in the Treaty of Lausanne of July 1923, and proclaimed the Republic of Turkey on 29 October 1923.

grand-principality-of-nizhny-novgorod-su.t: A powerful Volga principality that briefly rivalled Moscow and commissioned the Laurentian Codex of the Primary Chronicle.
grand-principality-of-nizhny-novgorod-su.o: Nizhny Novgorod was founded in 1221 at the meeting of the Oka and the Volga as a frontier fortress against Volga Bulgaria. In 1341 the Golden Horde granted it to Konstantin Vasilyevich of Suzdal, who moved his capital there and created a new grand principality.
grand-principality-of-nizhny-novgorod-su.r: The principality grew rich on Volga trade with the Horde and the East. Dmitry Konstantinovich held the grand-princely title of Vladimir from 1360 to 1363 before giving way to Dmitry Donskoy, who married his daughter Evdokia. In 1377 the monk Lavrenty copied the oldest surviving manuscript of the Primary Chronicle for him.
grand-principality-of-nizhny-novgorod-su.e: Raids by Tatar emirs and quarrels among Dmitry's brothers weakened the state. In 1392 Vasily I of Moscow bought the right to Nizhny Novgorod from Khan Tokhtamysh and annexed it to the Grand Duchy of Moscow, though the Suzdal princes struggled to regain it for decades.

grand-duchy-of-hesse.t: Hesse-Darmstadt as a grand duchy, a constitutional state on both banks of the Rhine and home of the Darmstadt Artists' Colony.
grand-duchy-of-hesse.o: Landgrave Louis X of Hesse-Darmstadt joined the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806 and took the title Grand Duke Louis I, gaining the Duchy of Westphalia and mediatised territories. In 1816 he exchanged Westphalia for Rhenish Hesse with Mainz and Worms on the left bank.
grand-duchy-of-hesse.r: A constitution of 1820 established a two-chamber parliament. The state combined Lutheran Upper Hesse and Starkenburg with Catholic Rhenish Hesse, and Mainz was a federal fortress. The family married into royal houses: Princess Alix became Empress Alexandra of Russia. Grand Duke Ernest Louis founded the Darmstadt Artists' Colony on the Mathildenhöhe in 1899, a centre of Jugendstil.
grand-duchy-of-hesse.e: Hesse sided with Austria in 1866 and lost Hesse-Homburg and some districts to Prussia, but survived and joined the German Empire. Ernest Louis was deposed in November 1918, and the state became the People's State of Hesse.

gallaecia.t: The late Roman province of north-western Iberia, created by Diocletian and soon to become the home of the Suebic kingdom.
gallaecia.o: Gallaecia was formed around 293 by Diocletian's reform, which split Hispania Tarraconensis into smaller provinces. It covered the lands of the Callaeci and Astures, from the Douro to the Bay of Biscay, with Bracara Augusta (Braga) as its capital.
gallaecia.r: A governor ran the province under the Diocese of Hispania. Its economy was rural, based on farming, herding and the remains of the gold-mining industry around Asturica Augusta. Towns such as Lucus Augusti (Lugo), with its surviving walls, were fortified in the late 3rd century. Christianity spread, and the ascetic movement of Priscillian, executed in 385, found strong support here.
gallaecia.e: In 409 Suebi and Hasding Vandals entered Gallaecia, and the Suebi made it the centre of their kingdom. Roman rule faded, as recorded by Hydatius, bishop of Aquae Flaviae, and the name lived on in the medieval Kingdom of Galicia.

ghaznavid-empire.t: A Turkic dynasty from Ghazni whose sultan Mahmud raided deep into India and whose court fostered Persian literature, including Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.
ghaznavid-empire.o: Sabuktigin, a Turkic slave soldier in the service of the Samanid Empire, became governor of Ghazni in 977. His son Mahmud seized Khurasan in 998 and threw off Samanid authority, gaining recognition from the Abbasid caliph.
ghaznavid-empire.r: Mahmud of Ghazni launched some seventeen raids into India between 1001 and 1026, defeating the Hindu Shahis and sacking Somnath, which brought vast wealth to Ghazni. The empire relied on a standing army of slave soldiers and war elephants, while Persian administration and culture flourished: the poet Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh, and al-Biruni wrote his study of India under Ghaznavid patronage.
ghaznavid-empire.e: The Seljuks defeated Mas'ud I at Dandanaqan in 1040, taking Khurasan. The Ghaznavids continued in eastern Afghanistan and the Punjab, ruling from Lahore after the Ghurid Sultanate sacked Ghazni in 1150, until the Ghurids took Lahore in 1186.

guarco.t: A coastal lordship of the Cañete valley that resisted the Incas for years, with its stronghold at Cerro Azul by the Pacific.
guarco.o: The lordship of Guarco, or Huarco, emerged in the lower Cañete valley south of Lima around 1100. It developed around fishing villages and irrigation, with a fortified centre at Cerro Azul, a headland on the Pacific coast, and the fortress of Ungará.
guarco.r: Guarco was ruled by local lords who controlled farmland and fishing. Excavations at Cerro Azul have shown large compounds used to store dried fish, especially anchovies and sardines, which were traded inland for farm goods. Society seems to have been organised around elite families who controlled food stores and labour.
guarco.e: According to the chronicler Pedro Cieza de León, Guarco resisted the Incas for several years in the time of Túpac Inca Yupanqui. After its fall around 1470 the Incas built the fortress and administrative centre of Incawasi in the Cañete valley. The region came under Spanish rule in the 1530s.

ganja-khanate.t: A khanate centred on the city of Ganja whose last khan, Javad Khan, died defending it against the Russian storm of 1804.
ganja-khanate.o: After Nader Shah's death in 1747, Shahverdi Khan of the Ziyadoghlu branch of the Qajar tribe, whose family had long governed Ganja and Karabakh for the Safavids, made Ganja an independent khanate. It covered the fertile plain between the Kura and the Lesser Caucasus.
ganja-khanate.r: The khans ruled a town of craftsmen and merchants and surrounding villages producing grain, silk and fruit. Pressed by the Karabakh Khanate and Georgia, the khanate paid tribute to Erekle II of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti for decades. Javad Khan, who ruled from 1786, rebuilt its strength and sided with Qajar Iran against Georgia and Russia.
ganja-khanate.e: In January 1804 Russian troops under Pavel Tsitsianov stormed Ganja, and Javad Khan was killed with his son. The Russian Empire annexed the khanate and renamed the city Elizavetpol; it regained the name Ganja in the 20th century.

gotland.t: Self-governing farmers' republic on the Baltic island of Gotland, rich from trade, which kept its own law and assembly until a Danish conquest in 1361.
gotland.o: Gotland's position in the middle of the Baltic made it a trading hub from the Iron Age. Its picture stones and more than 700 Viking Age silver hoards, including the Spillings hoard, show immense wealth from trade with Rus', the Islamic world and Western Europe. The Gutasaga records an agreement under which the islanders paid a yearly tribute to the king of the Svear in return for protection.
gotland.r: Free farmers governed themselves through the Gutnalthing, the island's general assembly, which met at Roma, and wrote down their own law, the Gutalag. Every farmer was also a trader, and Gotlanders held privileges in Novgorod and across the Baltic. In the 12th and 13th centuries the island was covered with stone churches, and Visby grew into a German-dominated Hanseatic town.
gotland.e: Tension between rural Gotlanders and Visby led to civil war in 1288. In 1361 Valdemar IV of Denmark invaded, massacring the farmers' army outside Visby. Gotland then passed among Denmark, pirates and the Teutonic Order, and became Swedish in 1645 by the Treaty of Brömsebro.

gangani-ireland.t: People of western Ireland recorded by Ptolemy near the Shannon estuary, sharing their name with the Gangani of north-west Wales.
gangani-ireland.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Gangani on the west coast of Ireland, south of the Auteini and north of the Velabri, usually located in County Clare or around the mouth of the Shannon. The same name is given to a headland in Wales, home of the Gangani (Britain), on the Llŷn peninsula.
gangani-ireland.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or customs. The shared name on both sides of the Irish Sea has been taken as evidence of migration, of an Irish group settled in Wales, or simply of a common Celtic word, perhaps connected with Irish legends of the Gamanrad, but none of these ideas can be proven.
gangani-ireland.e: The Gangani of Ireland do not appear in later sources. Their region later formed part of the Kingdom of Munster and the lands of peoples such as the Ui Fidgenti.

gibraltar.t: A British territory on the rock at the entrance to the Mediterranean, held since 1704 and still claimed by Spain.
gibraltar.o: An Anglo-Dutch fleet under Admiral George Rooke captured Gibraltar in 1704 during the War of the Spanish Succession, nominally for the Habsburg claimant Charles. Spain ceded the town and fortress to Great Britain in perpetuity by Article X of the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.
gibraltar.r: Gibraltar became a fortress and naval base guarding the Strait, surviving the Great Siege of 1779-1783 and serving as a key base in the Napoleonic and World Wars. Its mixed population of Genoese, Spanish, Maltese, Jewish and British origin developed a distinct identity and the Llanito speech. It became a Crown colony in 1830.
gibraltar.e: Spain pressed its claim at the UN; Gibraltarians voted to stay British in 1967, and Spain closed the land border from 1969 to 1985. In 2002 they rejected shared sovereignty. Today it is a self-governing British Overseas Territory, with its border regime negotiated after Brexit.

guge.t: A kingdom of western Tibet founded by descendants of the Tibetan emperors, whose kings sparked the revival of Buddhism in Tibet and whose ruined capital Tsaparang still stands.
guge.o: After the Tibetan Empire collapsed, Kyide Nyimagon, a descendant of its royal line, settled in western Tibet in the 10th century. His territories were divided among his sons, and one line ruled Guge and Purang in the upper Sutlej valley, later with its capital at Tsaparang.
guge.r: The kings Yeshe-Ö and Jangchub-Ö were great patrons of Buddhism. They founded Tholing monastery in 996, sent the translator Rinchen Zangpo to Kashmir and invited the Indian teacher Atisha, who arrived in 1042, beginning the later diffusion of Buddhism in Tibet. Guge grew rich on gold, wool and the trade across the Himalaya, and its temples hold outstanding murals.
guge.e: In 1624 the Jesuit António de Andrade founded a mission at Tsaparang with royal favour, angering the monastic establishment. In 1630 the Kingdom of Ladakh invaded with local support and ended the dynasty. Western Tibet passed to the Ganden Phodrang in the 1680s.

ghassanids.t: Christian Arab kings who guarded Byzantium's desert frontier for over a century and patronised the Miaphysite church in Syria.
ghassanids.o: The Ghassanids were part of the Azd, a tribal group that migrated north from South Arabia. Entering Roman territory in the late 5th century, they defeated the Salihids and around 502 made a treaty with the emperor Anastasius that made them the empire's chief Arab allies in Syria and Arabia.
ghassanids.r: Justinian made al-Harith ibn Jabala supreme phylarch and king over all Rome's Arab allies around 529 to counter the Lakhmids, Persia's clients; he killed the Lakhmid king al-Mundhir III in battle in 554. The Ghassanids moved between camps such as Jabiyah in the Golan, built churches and towers, and fervently supported Miaphysite Christianity, obtaining the consecration of Jacob Baradaeus as bishop. Their court attracted Arabic poets such as al-Nabigha and Hassan ibn Thabit.
ghassanids.e: In 581 the emperor Maurice arrested al-Mundhir ibn al-Harith and exiled him to Sicily, and the confederation fragmented. Restored under Heraclius, the Ghassanids fought for Byzantium at Yarmuk in 636; afterwards some accepted Islam and others, led by Jabala ibn al-Ayham, withdrew into Anatolia.

genoese-amasra.t: A Genoese trading colony on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia, protected by walls that still carry Genoese coats of arms.
genoese-amasra.o: After the Treaty of Nymphaeum of 1261 opened the Black Sea to Genoa, Genoese merchants established themselves at Amasra (Samastri), an old Byzantine port on a pair of headlands, which became one of their stations on the coast between Constantinople and Caffa.
genoese-amasra.r: Amasra was governed by Genoese consuls subordinate to the colonial authorities at Pera and Caffa. Its population was largely Greek, with Latin merchants and soldiers. The town traded in timber, grain and slaves and served as a harbour of refuge. The Genoese strengthened its castle, and their inscriptions and arms survive in the walls.
genoese-amasra.e: In 1460 Mehmed II appeared before Amasra and the Genoese surrendered without a fight. Much of the population was moved to Istanbul.

gath.t: Gath, the largest Philistine city in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE, home of Goliath in the Bible, destroyed by Aram-Damascus.
gath.o: Gath, at Tell es-Safi in the Judaean foothills, was a Canaanite town before Philistine settlers arrived in the 12th century BCE. It became one of the five cities of the Philistine Pentapolis, guarding the valley of Elah between the coastal plain and Judah.
gath.r: By the 10th century BCE Gath was the leading Philistine city, covering some 50 hectares. The Bible tells of its king Achish sheltering David and of the giant Goliath; an inscription found at the site contains two names resembling Goliath. Its temples show a mix of Aegean and local traditions.
gath.e: Around 830 BCE Hazael of Aram-Damascus besieged and destroyed Gath; the siege trench he dug has been excavated. The city never recovered its leading role.

government-of-national-unity.t: Arrow Cross regime of Ferenc Szálasi, installed by Germany in October 1944, which brought terror to Budapest in the final months of the war.
government-of-national-unity.o: On 15 October 1944 Regent Miklós Horthy announced that the Kingdom of Hungary (1920-1946) was seeking an armistice with the Soviet Union. Germany kidnapped his son and forced Horthy to abdicate in favour of Ferenc Szálasi, leader of the fascist Arrow Cross Party, who formed a Government of National Unity and took the title Leader of the Nation.
government-of-national-unity.r: The regime continued the war on Germany's side, mobilising every remaining resource. Arrow Cross militias murdered thousands of Budapest Jews, many shot into the Danube, and tens of thousands were sent on death marches towards Austria, while diplomats such as Raoul Wallenberg issued protective papers. A rival provisional government was formed at Debrecen under Soviet protection in December 1944.
government-of-national-unity.e: The Soviet siege of Budapest ended in February 1945, and Szálasi's government retreated west before collapsing in April 1945. Szálasi was captured by American troops, handed over to Hungary, and tried and executed in Budapest in 1946.

grand-duchy-of-wurzburg.t: Napoleonic grand duchy formed from the secularised bishopric of Würzburg for Ferdinand of Tuscany, a Habsburg in Napoleon's camp.
grand-duchy-of-wurzburg.o: The Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg was secularised in 1803 and given to Bavaria. Under the Peace of Pressburg in 1805, Bavaria handed it to Ferdinand III, former Grand Duke of Tuscany, in exchange for Salzburg, and it became the Electorate of Würzburg. Joining the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806, it was renamed a grand duchy.
grand-duchy-of-wurzburg.r: Ferdinand, a brother of Emperor Francis I, governed from the great baroque Würzburg Residenz, keeping a cultured court and a largely Catholic administration. The state was obliged to supply troops for Napoleon's campaigns, including the invasion of Russia in 1812. Wine growing on the Main was central to its economy.
grand-duchy-of-wurzburg.e: In 1814 Ferdinand recovered Tuscany, and Würzburg was returned to the Kingdom of Bavaria, becoming part of the province of Lower Franconia. Ferdinand's line, the Habsburg-Tuscany branch, ruled in Florence until 1859.

ghurid-sultanate.t: A dynasty from the mountains of Ghor in central Afghanistan that built the Minaret of Jam and laid the foundations of Muslim rule in northern India.
ghurid-sultanate.o: The Shansabani chiefs of Ghor, an isolated mountain region, were vassals of the Ghaznavids and Seljuks. In 1150 Ala al-Din Husayn sacked Ghazni, earning the name 'World Burner', and his nephews made Ghor an empire in the late 12th century.
ghurid-sultanate.r: The brothers Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, ruling from Firozkoh and Herat, and Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad of Ghor, ruling from Ghazni, divided their conquests. Ghiyath al-Din built the Minaret of Jam and the Herat mosque. Mu'izz al-Din defeated the Rajput Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain in 1192 and conquered northern India, leaving Turkic slave commanders such as Qutb al-Din Aybak in charge.
ghurid-sultanate.e: After Mu'izz al-Din's murder in 1206 the empire fragmented. Aybak founded the Delhi Sultanate, and the Khwarazmian Empire conquered Ghor and Ghazni by 1215.

getae.t: Thracian people of the lower Danube, followers of the god Zalmoxis, whose king Dromichaetes captured Lysimachus and whose lands formed the core of Dacia.
getae.o: Herodotus names the Getae among Thracians living south and north of the lower Danube when Darius I marched against the Scythians around 514 BCE; they alone resisted before being subdued. Their territory covered the Danube plain in modern Bulgaria and Romania.
getae.r: Getic chiefs and kings ruled from fortified centres; the royal city of Helis is often identified with Sveshtari, where a decorated tomb survives. Herodotus says the Getae believed in immortality through the god Zalmoxis. Grain, horses and trade with Greek Black Sea cities such as Histria shaped the economy. Around 292 BCE King Dromichaetes defeated and captured Lysimachus, then released him.
getae.e: Celtic incursions and pressure from Macedon and Rome fragmented Getic power. About 82 BCE Burebista united the Getae and Dacians into the Kingdom of Dacia; Roman writers afterwards used Getae and Dacians almost interchangeably.

golden-ambrosian-republic.t: A short-lived Milanese republic proclaimed when the Visconti line ended in 1447, which fell to its own general Francesco Sforza.
golden-ambrosian-republic.o: When Duke Filippo Maria Visconti died without a male heir in August 1447, a group of Milanese nobles and lawyers proclaimed a republic named after the city's patron saint Ambrose. Many subject cities of the Duchy of Milan seized the chance to break away.
golden-ambrosian-republic.r: The republic was led by elected captains and defenders of liberty, but split between nobles and popular leaders. Threatened by the Republic of Venice, it hired Francesco Sforza, husband of the late duke's illegitimate daughter Bianca Maria, who defeated the Venetians at Caravaggio in 1448. Sforza then made a separate peace with Venice and turned against Milan.
golden-ambrosian-republic.e: Sforza besieged the city, and in February 1450, with Milan starving, the citizens opened the gates. He was acclaimed duke, restoring the Duchy of Milan under the Sforza dynasty.

grand-principality-of-ryazan.t: A frontier principality on the Oka, first to fall to the Mongols in 1237 and the last major Russian land absorbed by Moscow.
grand-principality-of-ryazan.o: Ryazan on the middle Oka belonged to the Chernigov dynasty and was ruled together with Murom. Around 1129 the two lands separated, and Ryazan became a principality of its own under descendants of Yaroslav Sviatoslavich, bordering the steppe and the forest lands of the Mordvins.
grand-principality-of-ryazan.r: Its princes were frequently at war with Vladimir-Suzdal and later the Grand Duchy of Moscow, while facing steppe raids from the south. In December 1237 Batu's Mongols destroyed the old city and killed Prince Yuri Igorevich, an event later told in the tale of Evpaty Kolovrat. The capital moved to Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky, the modern city of Ryazan.
grand-principality-of-ryazan.e: Oleg Ivanovich, who ruled for most of 1350 to 1402, stood up to Dmitry Donskoy and kept out of the Battle of Kulikovo. Afterwards Moscow's influence grew steadily, and in 1521 Vasily III arrested Ivan Ivanovich, the last grand prince, and annexed Ryazan.

grand-duchy-of-posen.t: A Prussian province with limited Polish self-rule, created at the Congress of Vienna and stripped of its autonomy after the revolution of 1848.
grand-duchy-of-posen.o: At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 the western part of the Duchy of Warsaw, centred on Poznan, was returned to the Kingdom of Prussia. To reconcile its mainly Polish population, it was given the title of grand duchy and a promise of respect for Polish language and institutions.
grand-duchy-of-posen.r: The king of Prussia ruled through a Polish governor, Prince Antoni Radziwill, and the Polish language was used in schools and courts. After the November Uprising of 1830 in Congress Poland, the provincial president Eduard Flottwell began a policy of Germanisation. Polish landowners and clergy led a lively cultural and economic life, including the Bazar in Poznan.
grand-duchy-of-posen.e: In 1848 Ludwik Mieroslawski led a Polish uprising in the grand duchy, which Prussian troops crushed. Its special status was abolished, and it became the ordinary Province of Posen. In 1919 most of it passed to the Second Polish Republic.
