greuthungi.t: The eastern Goths of the Ukrainian steppe, whose realm under Ermanaric was shattered by the Huns and set off the great migrations.
greuthungi.o: Goths moving south-east from the Vistula reached the lands north of the Black Sea in the 3rd century, the land Jordanes called Oium. By the late 3rd century the Greuthungi, the 'steppe people', had emerged east of the Dniester, separate from the Tervingi to their west, and are linked to the Chernyakhov culture.
greuthungi.r: Ammianus Marcellinus describes the Greuthungi as ruled by kings, and their king Ermanaric was remembered as a mighty warrior whose dominion took in many peoples. Their society combined farming villages with a warrior aristocracy that raided and traded with the Roman world. Most remained pagan, though Gothic Christianity was spreading.
greuthungi.e: When the Huns attacked around 375, Ermanaric took his own life and his successor Vithimiris fell in battle. Many Greuthungi submitted to the Huns, while others under Alatheus and Saphrax crossed the Danube in 376 and helped crush the Romans at Adrianople in 378. Their descendants formed part of the later Ostrogoths.

gran-colombia.t: Bolívar's great republic uniting Venezuela, New Granada, Quito and Panama, which won independence for northern South America but broke apart in 1830.
gran-colombia.o: In December 1819, after Bolívar's victory at Boyacá, the Congress of Angostura proclaimed the Republic of Colombia, uniting Venezuela and New Granada. The Congress of Cúcuta adopted a centralist constitution in 1821, with Bolívar as president and Francisco de Paula Santander as vice-president. Panama joined in 1821, and Quito and Guayaquil in 1822.
gran-colombia.r: Santander governed from Bogotá while Bolívar campaigned in Peru and Upper Peru. The republic abolished the Indian tribute and passed a free-womb law in 1821. Regional resentment grew, especially in Venezuela, where José Antonio Páez led the Cosiata revolt in 1826. After the failure of the Convention of Ocaña in 1828, Bolívar assumed dictatorial powers and survived an assassination attempt that September.
gran-colombia.e: Venezuela under Páez seceded in 1830, followed by Ecuador under Juan José Flores. Bolívar resigned and died at Santa Marta in December 1830. In 1831 the remainder became the Republic of New Granada.

gerrha.t: A legendary trading city of eastern Arabia, described by Greek writers as the richest place in the world for its incense and spice trade.
gerrha.o: Gerrha is known mainly from Greek and Roman writers, who say it was founded by Chaldean exiles from Babylon on the Gulf coast of eastern Arabia. It flourished from around the 4th century BCE. Its site has never been identified with certainty; Thaj, Hofuf and the coast near Uqair have all been proposed.
gerrha.r: The Gerrhaeans carried frankincense and other goods from south Arabia across the desert and shipped Indian wares up the Gulf to Babylonia. Agatharchides and Strabo describe houses decorated with gold, silver and ivory. In 205 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus III sailed to Gerrha and accepted a tribute of silver, frankincense and myrrh in return for leaving it free. Local coins with Aramaic legends were struck in the region.
gerrha.e: Gerrha fades from the sources around the 1st century CE as Roman Red Sea trade and the Nabataean and Palmyrene routes took over. Its precise location remains one of the open questions of Arabian archaeology.

great-perm.t: A Komi principality on the upper Kama, Christianised by Saint Stephen of Perm and absorbed into Muscovy in 1505.
great-perm.o: The Komi-Permyak lands on the upper Kama were long a source of furs for Novgorod. In the late 14th century Saint Stephen of Perm converted many of the Komi and created the Old Permic alphabet for their language. By the mid 15th century the land was ruled by local princes dependent on Moscow, with Cherdyn as their centre.
great-perm.r: Great Perm was a land of forests, fur trapping and salt, linking the Russian north with the Urals and Siberia. Its princes, such as Mikhail Ermolaevich, were baptised and served the Grand Duchy of Moscow while ruling local communities. In 1472 Ivan III sent an army that took Cherdyn and tightened Moscow's control.
great-perm.e: Local princely rule lasted until 1505, when Moscow replaced Prince Matvey Mikhailovich with its own governor. The region became a base for the Stroganov family and for Russian expansion across the Urals into Siberia.

gezer.t: Gezer, a Canaanite city on the road from Egypt to Jerusalem, captured by pharaohs and, by biblical tradition, given to Solomon as a dowry.
gezer.o: Gezer lay on a hill at the edge of the Judaean foothills, overlooking the coastal road. In the Middle Bronze Age it was fortified with massive walls and gates, and a row of tall standing stones marked a cultic high place that still stands.
gezer.r: In the Late Bronze Age local kings ruled as vassals of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom. Thutmose III lists Gezer among his conquests, its kings Milkilu and Yapahu wrote Amarna letters, and the Merneptah Stele boasts that Gezer was seized. The Gezer calendar, an early Hebrew inscription, was found there.
gezer.e: Gezer kept its independence after the end of Egyptian rule until a pharaoh burned it, according to 1 Kings, and gave it to Solomon of the United Kingdom of Israel. Its later Israelite gate is often linked to that era.

ghassanid-kingdom.t: Christian Arab allies of Byzantium who guarded the desert frontier of Syria and patronised Miaphysite Christianity until the Islamic conquests.
ghassanid-kingdom.o: The Ghassanids were an Arab tribe said to have migrated from south Arabia to the Syrian desert margins, traditionally in the 3rd century. Around 500 they became Roman federates, and in 529 the emperor Justinian made al-Harith ibn Jabala supreme phylarch of the Arabs, giving the family authority over the allied tribes of the Byzantine Empire's eastern frontier.
ghassanid-kingdom.r: Ghassanid rulers led mobile cavalry against the Lakhmid Kingdom, ally of the Sasanian Empire, and policed the desert routes. They were committed Miaphysite Christians and protected that church against imperial pressure, sponsoring bishops and monasteries. Their camp at Jabiyah in the Golan and sites such as Rusafa served as courts, and poets such as al-Nabigha praised them.
ghassanid-kingdom.e: In 582 Byzantium arrested al-Mundhir ibn al-Harith and the federation broke up into rival chiefs. Revived partly against the Persians, Ghassanid forces fought for Byzantium at Yarmuk in 636 against the Rashidun Caliphate. Their last king, Jabala ibn al-Ayham, briefly converted to Islam, then withdrew to Byzantine Anatolia.

griqualand-west.t: The Griqua community of Griquatown under the Waterboer family, whose land claims became the legal key to the Kimberley diamond fields.
griqualand-west.o: Griqua, people of mixed Khoekhoe and settler descent from the Cape, had gathered at the London Missionary Society station of Klaarwater north of the Orange River. In 1813 the missionary John Campbell helped them adopt a written constitution and renamed the place Griquatown, under the leaders Adam Kok II and Barend Barends.
griqualand-west.r: The community was governed by elected kapteins and a council, with mission influence strong in law, schooling and church life. After Adam Kok II moved away, Andries Waterboer, kaptein from 1820, made a treaty with the Cape in 1834 that brought a small subsidy and guns. The Griqua lived by herding, hunting and trading, and spoke Cape Dutch.
griqualand-west.e: When diamonds were found in the late 1860s, Nicolaas Waterboer's claim to the diggings was upheld by the Keate Award, and Britain annexed the territory in 1871, creating the Griqualand West Colony around Kimberley.

galindians.t: The southernmost Baltic people of Prussia, living among the Masurian lakes and named by Ptolemy, whose land was almost empty by the time the Teutonic Knights arrived.
galindians.o: Ptolemy listed the Galindai in the 2nd century, and they are usually located in the lake country of southern Prussia, roughly modern Masuria in Poland. Like their neighbours the Sudovians and other Prussian groups, they lived in scattered clans around fortified hilltops, without any known central authority.
galindians.r: Almost nothing is recorded of their institutions. They farmed, fished and hunted in a land of forest and lakes, and shared the pagan religion and West Baltic speech of the Prussians. The Teutonic chronicler Peter of Dusburg claimed that Galindia had been depopulated by wars and famine long before his time.
galindians.e: By the late 13th century the area formed part of the great wilderness that the Teutonic Order absorbed during its conquest of Prussia, completed in 1283. Survivors were merged into the Prussian population, and the region was later resettled by German and Polish (Masurian) colonists.

genoese-famagusta.t: Genoese-held enclave around the great port of Famagusta in Cyprus, seized from the Lusignan kings in 1373 and held for ninety years.
genoese-famagusta.o: At the coronation of King Peter II of Cyprus in Famagusta in 1372, a dispute over precedence between Genoese and Venetian merchants led to riots in which Genoese were killed. Genoa sent a fleet in 1373, invaded the Kingdom of Cyprus and occupied Famagusta, keeping the city as security for a huge indemnity.
genoese-famagusta.r: Genoa governed Famagusta through a podesta and officials, and from 1447 through the Bank of Saint George, which ran it as a business. The once-thriving port declined as Genoa restricted the trade of the rest of the island and Mamluk and Turkish pressure grew. Many inhabitants left and the economy shrank.
genoese-famagusta.e: King James II of Cyprus, with Mamluk support, besieged Famagusta and recovered it in 1464, reuniting the island under the Lusignans. Its Gothic cathedral of Saint Nicholas and walls remain.

gortyn.t: Powerful city of the Mesara in southern Crete, famous for the Gortyn Code, the longest surviving early Greek law inscription.
gortyn.o: Gortyn grew in the early Iron Age on the Lethaios river at the western edge of the Mesara plain, near the older Minoan centre of Phaistos. By the 7th century BCE it was a Dorian city and, with Knossos, one of the two strongest powers on Crete.
gortyn.r: The Gortyn Code, inscribed c. 450 BCE on a wall later built into the Roman odeion, sets out laws on marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption and the status of slaves and serfs. Gortyn was ruled by kosmoi magistrates and had men's messes. In the Hellenistic period it fought Knossos and destroyed Phaistos c. 150 BCE.
gortyn.e: After the Roman conquest of 69 to 67 BCE, Gortyn, which had cooperated with Rome, became the capital of the province of Crete and Cyrenaica. It flourished under the Empire and the early Byzantines.

gallic-empire.t: Breakaway Roman state in Gaul, Britain and for a time Hispania, set up by Postumus in 260 when the empire seemed unable to defend its frontiers.
gallic-empire.o: In 260, after the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persians and Germanic invaders broke across the Rhine, the governor Postumus was proclaimed emperor by his troops at Cologne. He killed Gallienus' son Saloninus and won the loyalty of Gaul, Germania, Britain and Hispania.
gallic-empire.r: The Gallic emperors kept Roman institutions, with their own consuls, praetorian guard and mints at Cologne and Trier. They did not march on Rome but concentrated on defending the Rhine. Postumus was murdered by his troops in 269, followed by Marius, Victorinus and Tetricus I.
gallic-empire.e: Hispania returned to the central empire early, and Victorinus was murdered in 271. In 274 Aurelian defeated Tetricus near Châlons, where Tetricus seems to have abandoned his army. He was paraded in Aurelian's triumph and then given an office in Italy, and the provinces rejoined the Roman Empire.

graaff-reinet-republic.t: The first Boer republic, proclaimed by frontier farmers who drove out the Dutch East India Company's magistrate in 1795.
graaff-reinet-republic.o: Graaff-Reinet, the eastern frontier district of the Dutch Cape Colony, was in turmoil over the Company's handling of conflict with the Xhosa and the San. In February 1795 the burghers expelled the landdrost Honoratus Maynier and declared their independence, led by Adriaan van Jaarsveld and Marthinus Prinsloo.
graaff-reinet-republic.r: The rebels formed an assembly of national representatives, adopted the language of the French Revolution and demanded freedom to deal with Africans on their own terms, including enslaving captured San. They refused to recognise the Company's officials and, later, the authority of the British.
graaff-reinet-republic.e: After Britain took the Cape in 1795, it cut off supplies of ammunition, and the Graaff-Reinet burghers submitted in 1796. Further revolts broke out in 1799 and 1801, and the episode is often seen as a forerunner of the later Boer republics.

governorate-of-paraguay.t: The Spanish province centred on Asunción, best known for the Jesuit missions among the Guaraní and for the Comunero revolts against royal authority.
governorate-of-paraguay.o: In 1617 the crown divided the Governorate of the Río de la Plata in two. The northern part, with its capital at Asunción, became the Governorate of Paraguay, also known as Guayrá, covering the lands along the Paraguay and upper Paraná rivers.
governorate-of-paraguay.r: Paraguay was a poor, largely mestizo and Guaraní-speaking province. The Jesuits built a network of reductions among the Guaraní, which the bandeirantes of São Paulo raided in the 1620s and 1630s, forcing the missions south. Yerba mate was the chief export. Settlers resented the Jesuits' control of indigenous labour, and the Comunero revolts of 1721 to 1735, led at first by José de Antequera, challenged the viceroy's authority.
governorate-of-paraguay.e: Paraguay joined the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776 and became an intendancy in 1782. In 1811 it rejected the authority of Buenos Aires, defeated Manuel Belgrano's army, and in May overthrew the governor, becoming the independent Republic of Paraguay.

grand-duchy-of-finland.t: Autonomous Finland within the Russian Empire, where Finnish national identity, institutions and the first female suffrage in Europe took shape.
grand-duchy-of-finland.o: Russia conquered Finland from Sweden in the Finnish War of 1808-1809. At the Diet of Porvoo in 1809 Alexander I promised to respect Finland's laws, Lutheran religion and estates, and Finland became a grand duchy with the tsar as grand duke. The Treaty of Fredrikshamn confirmed the transfer, and in 1812 the capital moved from Turku to Helsinki.
grand-duchy-of-finland.r: Finland kept its Swedish-era laws and had its own Senate, civil service, army for a time and, from 1860, its own currency, the markka. Alexander II convened the Diet regularly and allowed Finnish to become an official language. Elias Lönnrot's Kalevala, published in 1835, inspired the national movement. In 1906 a unicameral parliament was created, elected by universal suffrage including women, the first in Europe.
grand-duchy-of-finland.e: From 1899 Russification threatened Finnish autonomy, and Governor-General Bobrikov was assassinated in 1904. After the Russian Revolution, the Finnish parliament declared independence on 6 December 1917, and Soviet Russia recognised it, creating the Republic of Finland.

grand-duchy-of-tuscany.t: The Medici and then Habsburg-Lorraine state of Tuscany, patron of Galileo and a pioneer of Enlightenment reform, including abolition of the death penalty.
grand-duchy-of-tuscany.o: In 1569 Pope Pius V raised Cosimo I de' Medici, ruler of the Duchy of Florence and conqueror of Siena, to the rank of Grand Duke of Tuscany, a title confirmed by the emperor in 1576.
grand-duchy-of-tuscany.r: The Medici grand dukes ran a centralised state from Florence. Ferdinando I made Livorno a free port open to Jews and foreign merchants, and Cosimo II made Galileo court mathematician. The Medici line ended in 1737; the last heiress, Anna Maria Luisa, left the family's art collections to Florence. Francis Stephen of Lorraine succeeded, and his son Peter Leopold reformed law and trade, abolishing torture and the death penalty in 1786.
grand-duchy-of-tuscany.e: Napoleon turned Tuscany into the Kingdom of Etruria in 1801 and annexed it to France in 1807. Restored in 1814, the Lorraine dynasty left when Leopold II fled in 1859, and Tuscany voted to join the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860.

great-moravia.t: The first major Slavic state in central Europe, where Cyril and Methodius created a Slavic liturgy and alphabet that shaped the Orthodox Slavic world.
great-moravia.o: Around 833 Prince Mojmír I of the Moravians drove Pribina out of Nitra and united the Slavs north of the middle Danube, creating a state centred on the Morava valley. Mojmír's successor Rastislav, installed with East Frankish help in 846, soon turned against East Francia and built a strong independent principality.
great-moravia.r: Great Moravia's power rested on large fortified centres such as Mikulčice, Staré Město and Pohansko, with stone churches and rich graves. In 863 Rastislav invited the Byzantine brothers Cyril and Methodius, who created the Glagolitic alphabet and Old Church Slavonic liturgy. Under Svatopluk I, the realm expanded into Bohemia, southern Poland and Pannonia.
great-moravia.e: After Svatopluk died in 894 his sons quarrelled and Bohemia broke away. Magyar invasions destroyed Great Moravia around 906 to 907; the last mention coincides with the Battle of Pressburg in 907. Its disciples carried the Slavic liturgy to Bulgaria, while its lands passed to the Duchy of Bohemia and Hungary.

german-confederation.t: Loose league of German states created at the Congress of Vienna, led by Austria and the arena of its rivalry with Prussia.
german-confederation.o: After Napoleon's fall the Congress of Vienna created the German Confederation in 1815 as a league of 39 sovereign states and free cities, including Austria and Prussia for their German lands and foreign monarchs for Hanover, Holstein and Luxembourg. Its Federal Diet met in Frankfurt under Austrian presidency.
german-confederation.r: The Confederation had no head of state or common government and existed mainly for mutual defence and order. Under Metternich it repressed liberalism through the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819. The Frankfurt Parliament of 1848-49 tried to replace it with a united German state but failed. Economic unity came instead through the Prussian-led Zollverein.
german-confederation.e: Prussia and Austria clashed over Schleswig-Holstein, and the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 ended the Confederation. Prussia formed the North German Confederation, from which the German Empire arose in 1871.

gadir.t: The great Phoenician city of Cádiz, gateway to the Atlantic, home of a famous temple of Melqart and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe.
gadir.o: Gadir was founded by settlers from Tyre on islands off the Atlantic coast near the mouth of the Guadalete. Ancient writers dated its foundation to around 1100 BCE, but archaeology places it in the 9th to 8th centuries BCE. Its position beyond the Strait of Gibraltar gave access to Tartessian silver and Atlantic tin.
gadir.r: Gadir was governed by its own elite under institutions modelled on Tyre, and its temple of Melqart, later identified with Hercules, drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean; Hannibal visited before marching on Italy in 218 BCE. Fish salting, purple dye and long-distance trade made it rich, and it came to lead the Phoenician towns of the south under Carthaginian hegemony.
gadir.e: In 206 BCE, after the Carthaginian defeat at Ilipa, Gadir went over to Rome under a treaty of alliance. Its citizens received Roman citizenship under Julius Caesar, and Gades became one of the wealthiest cities of Hispania Baetica.

granadine-confederation.t: Colombia's experiment with a confederation of sovereign states between 1858 and 1863, overthrown by a liberal civil war.
granadine-confederation.o: Pressure for federalism had grown in the Republic of New Granada, and Panama, Antioquia and other regions had become self-governing states. The constitution of 1858, under the conservative president Mariano Ospina Rodríguez, created the Granadine Confederation, a union of eight states with a weak central government in Bogotá.
granadine-confederation.r: The states had their own constitutions, armies and elections. Laws passed by Ospina's government to control state elections and armies were seen by liberals as an attack on state sovereignty. In 1860 Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera, governor of the State of Cauca, rebelled and declared Cauca separate from the confederation, starting a civil war.
granadine-confederation.e: Mosquera captured Bogotá in July 1861 and took power, expelling the Jesuits and confiscating church lands. The Rionegro Convention of 1863 replaced the confederation with the United States of Colombia.
